/politics/2026/sep/28/burnham-to-announc.headline: Burnham warns of ‘difficult decisions’ in budget as inflation rises to 3.1%
/politics/2026/sep/28/burnham-to-announc.excerpt: Andy Burnham has said “difficult decisions” will need to be taken in next month’s budget after a rise in energy prices triggered by the Iran war drove UK inflation above 3%. In a fresh blow for living standards amid the worsening damage to the global economy from the Middle East conflict, official figures showed soaring fuel prices pushed inflation from 2.9% in July to 3.1% in August. With the government under pressure as the fallout from the war rattles global financial markets, the prime minister signalled the 28 October budget would take into account investor fears over the hit to the public finances. “We will take difficult decisions to make sure the economy remains on track,” he said. “It is going to be challenging, because the picture around the world is challenging, particularly the situation in the Middle East, and we will look carefully at all those things. “We won’t take risks with people’s living standards or with the economy as a whole, so we will take it all into account.” The prime minister also downplayed criticism from Andy Haldane, who has urged him not to raise taxes.
/politics/2026/sep/28/burnham-to-announc.trail: PM rejects claim he leads a ‘tax-and-spend’ government, as Bank of England prepares for interest rates decision

/politics/2026/sep/28/burnham-to-announc.headline: No more UK energy bills support likely before price cap rise
/politics/2026/sep/28/burnham-to-announc.excerpt: Households are unlikely to receive further energy bills support before the October price cap, though more targeted measures could be looked at if there is a further shock in January, government sources said. Gas and electricity prices will rise by 4% from October under the new cap. The government has already removed VAT from domestic electricity bills to save average households £45 a year, a move announced in Andy Burnham’s first week in office. Prices had climbed by 13% at the start of July to take account of global energy market price rises caused by the US war on Iran and the closure of the strait of Hormuz. Burnham said on Wednesday that rising energy bills were “difficult for people and I recognise that” but he stopped short of promising intervention beyond the VAT cut, saying the government “would continue to look as we go forward at how we get energy prices down in the long term”. Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, said bills were being driven up by the Iran war and the government would “keep looking at what more we can do to protect families from unaffordable bills”. The chancellor, John Healey, said the government would look again towards the end of the year at whether more support was needed. “No government can stop the squeeze felt by families and businesses with a global shock of this magnitude. It’s being felt around the world.
/politics/2026/sep/28/burnham-to-announc.trail: Andy Burnham stops short of pledging further help as gas and electricity prices due to increase by 4% in October

/politics/2026/sep/28/burnham-to-announc.headline: UK inflation rises to 2.9% as Iran war drives up energy bills
/politics/2026/sep/28/burnham-to-announc.excerpt: UK inflation rose to 2.9% in July as the impact of the Iran war on energy prices triggered a renewed cost of living squeeze for British households. The Office for National Statistics said inflation rose from a 15-month low of 2.6% in June, driven by the rising price of gas and electricity. Matching City economists’ forecasts, it was the first rise in the annual rate as measured by the consumer prices index since March. Underscoring the challenge for Andy Burnham’s government to give “breathing space” to hard-pressed households, the acceleration in price rises comes after consumers in Great Britain faced the sharpest summer increase in energy bills in four years in July after the US-Israel war on Iran sent shock waves through global energy markets. The 13% increase in the cap on energy bills at the start of July led to a rise in gas and electricity bills. The ONS said consumers faced other pressures alongside the biggest jump in gas prices since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, including furniture prices falling by less than usual for this time of year, and a smaller fall in clothing prices because of reduced discounting. However, the prices of raw materials and goods leaving factories slowed, driven by a drop in crude oil and refined petroleum prices in July.
/politics/2026/sep/28/burnham-to-announc.trail: Accelerating price increases in July add to pressure on households, with chancellor saying ‘there is more to do to restore hope’

/politics/2026/sep/28/burnham-to-announc.headline: Thom Yorke, Romy and Brian Eno among 200 musicians urging PM to reject new North Sea drilling
/politics/2026/sep/28/burnham-to-announc.excerpt: More than 200 musicians including Massive Attack and Brian Eno have written to Andy Burnham urging him to reject plans for more oil and gas drilling in the North Sea. The letter, signed by 211 artists such as Bobby Gillespie, Olly Alexander and Paris Paloma, called on the prime minister to reject the Rosebank oilfield, warning that the project would fail to lower energy bills or provide energy security as most of the oil was likely to be exported. Other performers who put their name to the missive include Radiohead’s Thom Yorke, Ed O’Brien and Philip Selway; the Cure’s Robert Smith; Bobby Gillespie of Primal Scream; Alexis Taylor of Hot Chip; Anoushka Shankar, Kevin Rowland, Anna Calvi, Jacob Collier, David Gray, the electronic duo Bicep and the xx singer Romy. The government’s consultation on the project, which lies about 80 miles north-west of the Shetland Islands, closed on Monday. Ministers will now decide on its future as well as that of the Jackdaw gasfield off Aberdeen, whose consultation concluded a week ago. Adura, the company behind both projects, has said the projects would result in £10.8bn in investment and support 3,500 jobs at the peak of construction, with 880 employees over its production lifetime. However, environmental activists argue that extracting fossil fuels from the UK’s largest remaining untapped oilfield will accelerate climate chaos.
/politics/2026/sep/28/burnham-to-announc.trail: Robert Smith, Olly Alexander and Paris Paloma also among signatories to letter saying exploitation of Rosebank and Jackdaw fields defies climate reality

/politics/2026/sep/28/burnham-to-announc.headline: New UK cost of living crisis looms with soaring energy bills forecast to lift inflation
/politics/2026/sep/28/burnham-to-announc.excerpt: British households are facing a renewed cost of living squeeze, with official figures expected to show this week that soaring energy bills drove up inflation in July to close to 3%. As the Iran war continues to send shock waves through global energy markets, economists predict the surge in UK gas and electricity bills last month will push Britain’s headline inflation rate to 2.9%. In a fresh squeeze on household budgets, the figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) due on Wednesday are forecast to show a jump from a rate of 2.6% in June. The Bank of England is considering raising interest rates from as early as September in response to fears over stubbornly high inflation becoming entrenched in the economy. Reports also emerged overnight that the water regulator Ofwat was considering plans to impose “surge pricing” on water usage during droughts. It could see customers charged more for water use during summer and less in winter, or else charged higher prices when they pass a threshold of water use, according to the Daily Telegraph. The latest snapshot will highlight the challenge facing Andy Burnham’s government to ease the financial pressure on households and businesses before a difficult autumn budget. Economists said a rise in inflation as measured by the consumer prices index was likely after Ofgem, the energy regulator, lifted its cap on household gas and electricity bills by 13% in July.
/politics/2026/sep/28/burnham-to-announc.trail: Latest reading on Wednesday likely to frame scale of challenge for new PM to ease pressures on households amid Iran war fallout

/uk-news/2026/sep/29/intimidatory-far-ri.headline: Farmer who alerted police to RAF Fairford suspected bomb plot says there was ‘no follow-up’
/uk-news/2026/sep/29/intimidatory-far-ri.excerpt: A farmer who claims to have alerted the police to a suspected terrorist bomb plot at RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire has said she has had “no follow-up at all” from the authorities. The woman told reporters on Monday that she did not see herself as a hero for having reported vans blocking a road near the base while on her way back from a party. Five men from London were arrested in the village of Whelford, near to RAF Fairford, on Sunday on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offences. The village remained shut off on Monday afternoon, with people evacuated from their homes dispersed to family, friends, hotels and a leisure centre. The farmer, in her 50s, said she had been travelling home with her husband and a “young lad” who works for them when she spotted the vehicles parked in a “really strange formation”. She said: “You couldn’t drive between them on the road, and you also couldn’t drive up the farm drive, and I think this has been one of the funny things that people are saying: ‘How could you notice?’ But when you live in Whelford, you notice everything. We all know what cars each other drive, we know who we are, we know the people that cycle through regularly.” She said one of the vans had some “strange sign writing on it” and she initially believed it belonged to undercover police.
/uk-news/2026/sep/29/intimidatory-far-ri.trail: Woman who spotted suspicious vans and masked men says authorities did not contact her after five men were arrested

/uk-news/2026/sep/29/intimidatory-far-ri.headline: Schools forced to shut amid burst Thames Water pipe ‘leaking 750 litres a second’
/uk-news/2026/sep/29/intimidatory-far-ri.excerpt: Schools, businesses and homes across seven boroughs in England were hit by a Thames Water outage on Monday, from a burst water main reportedly leaking 750 litres a second. About 6,000 properties across five south London boroughs and two Surrey boroughs had no water supply or low pressure, Thames Water said. Thames Water apologised for the lack of water. A spokesperson said: “Our specialist team is now on site and working to stop the water flooding from the broken pipe.” Schools and colleges were forced to close across the boroughs. Esher College, a sixth-form college for 2,000 students, was among those forced to send pupils home and shut their doors. The college said: “Due to a major water outage effecting the KT10 area and our campus we are closed on Monday 28 September.” Kingston grammar school also closed, as did Long Ditton infant and nursery school, Thames Ditton infant school and Hollyfield school and sixth-form centre in Surbiton. Monica Harding, the Liberal Democrat MP for Esher and Walton, Surrey, said it was her understanding that water was leaking at 750 litres a second early on Monday morning after a large main burst. The community was left without water from about 5am. “It is completely unacceptable,” she said.
/uk-news/2026/sep/29/intimidatory-far-ri.trail: Leak causes outages and low pressure in parts of London and Surrey, affecting 6,000 properties and leaving some without water

/uk-news/2026/sep/29/intimidatory-far-ri.headline: UK security forces were aware of RAF Fairford suspected bomb plot, hints defence secretary
/uk-news/2026/sep/29/intimidatory-far-ri.excerpt: UK security services were aware in advance about a group of men arrested in connection with a suspected bomb plot against an RAF base used by the US military, Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, has indicated. Five men were arrested on suspicion of terrorism offences after armed officers found explosives in three vans parked minutes from RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, from which the US air force flies missions against Iran. Police were alerted after a local woman driving near the base in the early hours of Sunday saw the vans and men acting unusually and called 999. Speaking to the BBC on Monday morning, the woman said security services had seemingly “really dropped the ball on this”. Speaking later to BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, Streeting said that while he wanted to thank the woman – who has chosen to remain anonymous – for calling police, she had “a partial picture”. He praised police and security services for their work, referencing comments by Donald Trump who claimed the suspects had been under view for a long time. Trump alleged the men “were looking to do big damage” and said of the response: “It was fantastic. Working with Britain, it was an amazing job.” Streeting, when asked if he was saying Trump had been correct, did not reject this.
/uk-news/2026/sep/29/intimidatory-far-ri.trail: Wes Streeting indicates farmer who alerted police and said security forces had ‘dropped the ball’ only ‘had a partial picture’

/society/2026/sep/28/high-screen-usage-i.headline: At Climate Week, Elmo recalls a storm on Sesame Street: ‘Courage is when you still help others’
/society/2026/sep/28/high-screen-usage-i.excerpt: A generation of political leaders has failed to galvanize sufficient action on the climate crisis for so long now that it was perhaps little surprise that an audience in New York City turned to a three-and-a-half-year-old red furry monster for inspiration on Tuesday. Elmo, the Sesame Street denizen, made a starry appearance at a Climate Week event that highlighted how the impacts of global heating affect children. The red creature, who frequently refers to himself in the third person, recounted to the audience his fear when a storm hit Sesame Street, an event depicted in a recent episode that featured the singer Post Malone. “We all feel scared sometimes, but courage is when you feel scared but you still help others,” Elmo said at the event, which was named “Big Storms, Big Feelings”. “I tried to help others by giving lots of hugs and playing music on Elmo’s xylophone. When the storm passed Sesame Street didn’t look like Sesame Street, there was trash and branches all over the place.” Elmo revealed that, much like a prepper, he had a “go bag” ready for the disaster and that the residents of Sesame Street banded together to help their neighborhood clean up after the storm. “Home is the people who make the place special,” he added. “So long as you’re with the people you love, you’ll be home.
/society/2026/sep/28/high-screen-usage-i.trail: New York event hears about the red Muppet’s fears during a recent storm as climate crisis increasingly affects children

/society/2026/sep/28/high-screen-usage-i.headline: Trump officials sending undocumented children to Texas sparks fears of mass deportation
/society/2026/sep/28/high-screen-usage-i.excerpt: The Trump administration has started sending a majority of undocumented children who came to the US alone and have new immigration court cases to Texas, where government facilities for them are unlicensed, their chances of getting a lawyer are low and advocates fear that “a deportation churn-out factory” awaits them, the Guardian has learned. Almost 80% of children in federal custody who arrived unaccompanied by a parent or legal guardian and who were placed in immigration court proceedings in July – and over 90% in August – have been funneled into shelter networks somewhere in Texas, a dramatic upswing from the months prior, according to analysis shared exclusively with the Guardian from researchers at the immigration data insights platform bklg.org. This is understood to amount to a total of 925 children in the care of the Health and Human Services (HHS) department’s office of refugee resettlement (ORR) and in open immigration court proceedings based in Texas, with 651 sent there in July and August alone. Federal officials’ sudden shift toward ushering these vulnerable kids to the Republican-controlled, deeply conservative state for no publicly stated reason has alarmed immigrants’ rights advocates amid concerns about their treatment and access to due process under US laws.
/society/2026/sep/28/high-screen-usage-i.trail: Exclusive: Nearly 90% of children in federal custody being directed to GOP-controlled state that has unlicensed facilities and low legal representation rates

/society/2026/sep/28/high-screen-usage-i.headline: A spoonful of sugar: how South Africa’s weigh-and-pay shops are tackling ‘poverty tax’ head on
/society/2026/sep/28/high-screen-usage-i.excerpt: Every morning, on her way to the laundry shop she runs in Johannesburg’s Alexandra township, Tsholofelo Mphela stops at a bright yellow shipping container to buy a few spoonfuls of sugar. Inside, shelves are lined with large jars of beans, rice and maize meal, and clear boxes filled with breakfast cereal and loose teabags. A tap dispenses cooking oil by the millilitre. The cashier weighs Mphela’s purchase before ringing it up for a few rand. She is the sole breadwinner for a family of eight, and her monthly bulk grocery shop lasts only about a week. “At times, I don’t have enough money to buy a 2kg bag of sugar,” Mphela says. A 2kg bag costs about 60 rand (£2.80). At the weigh-and-pay shop Gcwalisa – which means “fill up” in isiZulu – designed to tackle malnutrition in one of South Africa’s poorest communities, she can buy exactly what she can afford. South Africa has a rich agricultural sector and produces more than enough food to feed its entire population. Yet millions of people still struggle with hunger. A 2024 national survey found that nearly two-thirds of all households were affected by food insecurity, and nearly 30% of children under five suffered from stunting linked to chronic malnutrition. Healthy food remains out of reach for many, contributing to issues such as widespread obesity and diabetes – which recently overtook HIV and tuberculosis as the No 1 cause of natural death in the country.
/society/2026/sep/28/high-screen-usage-i.trail: Run by a social enterprise, the six shops operate from shipping containers across Johannesburg’s Alexandra township and sell food and household goods by weight in small, affordable amounts

/society/2026/sep/28/high-screen-usage-i.headline: Russell Howard announces ‘devastating’ death of baby son
/society/2026/sep/28/high-screen-usage-i.excerpt: Russell Howard has announced the death of his baby son, in what he described as the “most devastating time of our lives”. The 46-year-old comedian said his family had been “changed for ever” after their “beautiful baby boy”, Felix, died shortly after birth. In a statement on his Instagram account, Howard said: “During the most devastating time of our lives, the hospital staff who cared for us showed extraordinary compassion, kindness and humanity. They helped us navigate an unimaginable heartache and gave us support when we needed it most.” Howard praised the support he and his wife, Cerys Morgan, had received from a bereavement midwife named Lauren, who he said had experienced a similar tragedy. “Her care meant more to us than we can ever put to words,” he added. “During our time in hospital, Felix was placed in a cool cot, which meant that my wife and I were able to spend precious hours with our beautiful boy. “Those hours are among the most precious memories we have of Felix.” Howard and Morgan, who is an NHS doctor, have set up the Felix Foundation, in memory of their son, to help other families facing the same “devastating circumstances”. To help launch the foundation, Howard will host a special charity gala at the O2 in London on 8 February featuring a lineup of friends and colleagues made up of Michael McIntyre, Jimmy Carr, Aisling Bea, Guz Khan, Greg Davies, Mo Gilligan, Michelle Wolf and John Bishop.
/society/2026/sep/28/high-screen-usage-i.trail: Comedian and his wife, Cerys Morgan, set up charitable foundation in memory of Felix, who died shortly after birth

/society/2026/sep/28/high-screen-usage-i.headline: Quarter of branded baby foods in UK still have too much sugar, analysis finds
/society/2026/sep/28/high-screen-usage-i.excerpt: Almost a quarter of popular branded baby foods sold in UK supermarkets still contain excessive amounts of sugar, analysis suggests, a year after the government introduced voluntary industry guidelines. In August 2025 the government gave baby food manufacturers 18 months to reduce the sugar and salt content of their products, stop marketing snacks to infants under 12 months, and address misleading and inaccurate labelling that makes some infant foods appear healthier than they actually are. An analysis of 224 branded infant foods and snacks has found that, a year on, more than half (58%) breached at least one of the nine guidelines and that a quarter of all products breached two or more. Nora Cavani, the chief executive and co-founder of Alba Health, a gut health company that conducted the analysis, said: “Parents are not failing their children – they are being misled. Products that contain more sugar than a child should consume in a day are sold under the banner of health and nature. A year on from the guidelines’ introduction, the data shows voluntary standards haven’t worked.” The foods studied included purees, breakfast, main meals, desserts, snacks and finger foods made by nine of the UK’s leading brands: Ella’s Kitchen, Heinz, Organix, HiPP, Kiddylicious, Little Freddie, Piccolo, Aptamil and Cow & Gate. Of these, 51 (23%) contained too much sugar, including 52% of Kiddylicious’s products, 28% of Piccolo’s, 27% of Heinz’s, and 24% of Little Freddie products.
/society/2026/sep/28/high-screen-usage-i.trail: Exclusive: Of 224 branded infant foods and snacks, more than half breached guidelines brought in a year ago

/football/2026/sep/28/manchester-city-ch.headline: Mancini refers to ‘double’ Manchester City contract and says it ‘isn’t my problem’
/football/2026/sep/28/manchester-city-ch.excerpt: Roberto Mancini appeared to admit having “a double contract” while managing Manchester City, but insisted the club are not guilty after being found to have breached Premier League financial rules. Mancini led City to their first Premier League title in 2012 during his four-year spell in Manchester. Now in charge of the Italy national team, he described the scandal surrounding the club as “not a problem that concerns me”. One element of the case against City is an investigation into payment details for players and managers between 2009 and 2018. The German magazine Der Spiegel obtained evidence that Mancini doubled his base salary of £1.45m by advising a club in Abu Dhabi. “It’s not a problem that concerns me,” the 61-year-old said in Italy’s press conference before their Nations League match with Turkey on Monday. “It’s not something new because every four or five years this comes up. Manchester City is not guilty and the fact of having a double contract isn’t my problem but theirs, probably.” Mancini lifted the FA Cup as well as the Premier League during his time at City, the first trophies of Sheikh Mansour’s ownership, laying the foundations for future success. He left in 2013 after defeat against Wigan in the FA Cup final. City have been found guilty by an independent commission of the vast majority of more than 100 charges related to alleged breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules.
/football/2026/sep/28/manchester-city-ch.trail: Roberto Mancini has appeared to acknowledge he had ‘a double contract’ when he managed Manchester City

/football/2026/sep/28/manchester-city-ch.headline: Ever feel you’ve been cheated? Consequences could be profound after Manchester City guilty verdict
/football/2026/sep/28/manchester-city-ch.excerpt: So it turns out none of that was real. Nothing that happened in English football between 2009‑10 and 2017-18 that involved Manchester City actually happened. City beating Manchester United 6-1 at Old Trafford? Fake. Sergio Agüero’s 94th‑minute winner to clinch the title in 2012? A figment of the imagination. That season City reached 100 points? Bobby Ewing dreamed it in the shower. Without those successes, City wouldn’t have been in the position they were for the past eight seasons (and 35 of the charges relate to a failure to cooperate with Premier League investigations between 2018 and 2023). The 14 successive wins that took them to the league title in 2018-19 would not have happened without what went before. Neither would the Treble of 2023 or the record four league titles in a row. So while it may turn out that those successes did indeed happen, they are tainted by what went before. “We’re not really here”? Turns out none of us have been for quite some time. There will be an appeal. This is not yet the final truth, which could still be a long way off. But it may turn out that Jürgen Klopp was a lot more successful than anybody thought, that Brendan Rodgers and Ole Gunnar Solskjær are title‑winning managers. Probably not, because the authorities seem reluctant, even if titles are stripped from a club, to reallocate those titles – and understandably: if one side is streaking clear, priorities for others change.
/football/2026/sep/28/manchester-city-ch.trail: The Premier League could be hit hard by the aftermath of this case, while Manchester City fans may know they took 30 years to recover from a guilty verdict of illegal payments in 1906

/football/2026/sep/28/manchester-city-ch.headline: Manchester City chair al-Mubarak insists ‘nothing has changed’ after guilty verdict
/football/2026/sep/28/manchester-city-ch.excerpt: Khaldoon al-Mubarak, the Manchester City chair, has spoken for the first time since the club was found guilty on virtually all counts of breaching Premier League financial rules. He said “nothing has changed” and “our confidence and intent in proving the club’s innocence is just as strong as when this began”. News broke on Friday that City had been found guilty on all but one of the 115 charges laid by the Premier League in February 2023, charges the club have always strenuously denied. The club did not comment on the verdict until Saturday afternoon when al-Mubarak said on social media: “While some people have been quick to reach their own conclusions, and there is so much noise swirling around us, nothing has changed. We have faced challenges together before and have prevailed. There remain many who want to undermine the momentum of our club. We will not give them that opportunity. “We have some exciting moments to look forward to after this international break. We travel to Anfield in a fortnight and then host Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League back at Etihad Stadium – moments that give us an opportunity to celebrate the strength of the Manchester City family. Thank you, as always, for your constant support.” Earlier, City’s manager, Enzo Maresca, posted a cryptic message on social media reading “I know nothing”. On Saturday morning, Maresca was approached for comment about whether he is seeking reassurance from the club on their continued stance of innocence.
/football/2026/sep/28/manchester-city-ch.trail: Manchester City’s chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, has attempted to dismiss the club’s guilty verdict as ‘noise’

/football/2026/sep/28/manchester-city-ch.headline: Manchester City verdict: what happens next, will club appeal and could they be relegated?
/football/2026/sep/28/manchester-city-ch.excerpt: What happens next? Manchester City have been found guilty of the vast majority of the 134 disciplinary charges brought against them by the Premier League. In keeping with the history of this case which has been conducted exclusively in private and with every party sworn to secrecy, there is a lot we don’t know. We do not even have an official confirmation that the three-person judicial panel has reached a verdict. All of football is acting as if they have, however, and that reports of a big win for the Premier League are correct. If these assumptions are accurate, and neither party have formally denied them at least, then the immediate thing to watch out for is news of an appeal. Under Premier League rules, City would have 14 days from the announcement of the verdict to submit an appeal and the process that follows should be completed in less than 12 weeks from then. Once the appeal has been heard – which should happen in one block of no more than five days – and a verdict reached, the appeal panel are also expected to publish written reasons behind their decisions. We should also see the written reasons from the original judicial panel too, but the unique scale of this case has meant that normal procedures have not always been followed, and the date of publication for these reasons remains unknown. If City do appeal, what happens? The club would be submitting an appeal based solely on the decision and not any resulting punishment, which is yet to be determined.
/football/2026/sep/28/manchester-city-ch.trail: We analyse what City must do to appeal, why even that might not be the end of the legal wrangling, and the potential penalties if the verdict is upheld

/football/2026/sep/28/manchester-city-ch.headline: Everything you need to know about Manchester City’s hearing and charges
/football/2026/sep/28/manchester-city-ch.excerpt: What has happened? An independent panel has found Manchester City guilty on almost all of more than a 100 charges of breaking Premier League competition rules between the seasons 2009-10 and 2022-23. The panel found they had acted in bad faith and broken numerous rules over financial fair play. City, meanwhile, say the process is continuing and it is understood the club intend to appeal against the guilty verdict. Was this the result of ‘Football Leaks’? Uefa found City in breach of its financial fair play regulations in 2014 but reached a settlement under which City paid a €20m (£17m) fine and submitted reduced squads to the Champions League. The revisiting of alleged irregularities came after the document hack known as “Football Leaks” in 2015 exposed what appear to be official documents and email communication from inside City, alongside a number of other football organisations. The allegations against City were published in 2018. These documents are understood to also have prompted the Premier League’s investigation, a four-year process which brought the charges. City have previously described Football Leaks as an “orchestrated campaign” and part of “an endless attempt to damage us”. What are the accusations? In February 2023 the Premier League charged the club with more than 100 rule breaches, after investigating the club since December 2018.
/football/2026/sep/28/manchester-city-ch.trail: The club have been found guilty by an independent panel on almost all of more than 100 Premier League charges but are intending to appeal the verdict

/uk-news/2026/sep/28/merseyside-blaze-ki.headline: Woman and three children killed after ‘intense’ fire ravages Merseyside house
/uk-news/2026/sep/28/merseyside-blaze-ki.excerpt: A woman and three children have died after an overnight fire ripped through a semi-detached house on Merseyside. The Merseyside fire and rescue service (MFRS) said crews arrived at the blaze in Bootle at about 3.45am on Tuesday. Speaking at the scene, the chief fire officer, Nick Searle, said four people inside the house had died and another person, outside the property, had been taken to hospital. He said the fire was “intense” and “spread very rapidly”. Four people were discovered in an upstairs bedroom showing no signs of life, a fire service spokesperson said. At the fire’s height, six crews were on the scene and eight firefighters entered the house, which was alight when they arrived, they added. One local person, who did not want to be named, said: “We all came out on the front and we could see smoke coming over from the houses. The sirens woke me up and there were fire engines in the street.” Another person said: “I heard shouting in the early hours but I just thought someone was having an argument, then I came downstairs and saw all the fire engines.” At the scene, Searle said: “Firstly, our thoughts are with everyone who’s been affected by the tragic incident this morning.” He said the MFRS control room received a 999 call at 3.38am and crews from surrounding stations were mobilised, with the first fire engine arriving at 3.45am to find the house “well alight”.
/uk-news/2026/sep/28/merseyside-blaze-ki.trail: One other person being treated in hospital after fire crews respond to early-hours incident at home in Bootle
